*Zhīyuǎn Yíbiān*, Volume One.
The Chapter on the Substance of the Precepts by the Śramaṇa Yuanzhao of Yuhang Prefecture.
On the day of the latter summer retreat in the third year of the Xining era, the Śramaṇa Yuanzhao [commented] upon the *Karmavācanā-vibhāṣā* of the Southern Mountain Patriarch.

I have excerpted the "Chapter on the Precept-Substance" (*śīla-tattva*). Looking back at the former sages and forward to the later disciples, their debates have been passed down in succession, with points of success and failure appearing alternately;
therefore, I shall here set forth the general outline directly.

Now, the essence of the precepts (*śīla*) is the pivotal core of the Vinaya section, the fundamental basis for upholding or violating them, the primary source for reversing the flow [of saṃsāra], and the precursor to the initiation of practice.
However, because these teachings have remained obscure and their principles are profound and deep, they were transmitted through nine dynasties.
From time to time, illustrious sages have appeared; though each displayed their own distinct path, none were heard to have reached a definitive resolution of the ultimate meaning.

Upon reaching the Tang dynasty, it was my own Patriarch alone who exhausted the mysteries and perfected the nature of reality. He reviewed the teachings of antiquity, rejected all that was superficial and false, and analyzed the fundamental tenets.

He weighed and refined the principles of doctrine, clearly manifesting the Three Schools. Truly, he may be called one who gathered the source of the teachings of a single transformation and awakened the wisdom of the masses who were lost in delusion.
This is the case. However, since the Sage Teacher has passed away, while the texts remain, the underlying principles are obscured.

Consequently, six or seven schools have emerged, each asserting its own private interpretations as the guiding manual; yet, being uncertain of their direction and lacking any definitive ground, they offer no benefit to future generations, and thus none of them are cited here.
At this time, Zilong also emerged from the Zhang school, claiming that according to the *Yeshu*, the three schools establish their essential natures (*titi*). He once...
Examining the beginning and end [of these errors], it is found that they succeed in refuting others but fail in self-understanding.

The reason one must now refute them is that their names and characteristics are confused, and because the scholars of various schools were deluded at the time. Therefore, I shall briefly censure four faults to distinguish right from wrong: first, the confusion between the Great and Small Vehicles;

second, the deviation from the partial toward the Perfect meaning; third, the arbitrary division of two distinct entities; and fourth, the unauthorized concealment of the sacred texts. First, regarding the Great [Vehicle]:

As for those who are confused and muddled: they claim that the provisional school of the *Four-Part Vinaya* takes seeds as its essence (the *Zenghui* commentary is likewise; it merely distinguishes them by taking the functional capacity upon the seeds).
Now, even seeds are not something discussed in the provisional or superficial teachings of the sūtras and śāstras, let alone in the Hīnayāna vinaya sections.
Furthermore, if it is claimed that the provisional basis (*jia-zong*) is the seed, then what is this entity that is neither form (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*)?

Moreover, since the provisional basis is already said to be the seed, what would be the purpose of establishing the precept-body (*śīla-tattva*) in the subsequently established Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*)?

Such false assertions confuse and disorder the fundamental tenets of the teachings and cannot be lightly excused. Second, regarding the partial deviation from the meaning of "Perfection" (*yuan*): "Perfection" means to be pervasive, harmonious, and all-encompassing; it is not...

"Different" (*yi*) does not mean "partial. That [text] explains the precept-substance (*śīla-tattva*) of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), stating: "Due to the seeds produced by karma, they permeate the fundamental storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and remain forever as seeds;

this is precisely the precept-substance. This is unlike the Provisional Teachings (*jiazong*), which posit seeds externally [as a separate entity]. (If one asks: "How could the Provisional Teachings ever claim that seeds constitute the substance?

Furthermore, since seeds are singular, how can it be said they are 'different'?"—the answer is that the point is not about the nature of the seeds themselves, but their ontological status. Since it is said to be "different," how can it be called the meaning of the "Perfect"? It further states: "From the shallow to the..."

Profound! The three schools have alternately fallen into disuse; since they tolerate one another’s displacement, can this truly be called "perfect" (*yuan*)? My current explanation of the meaning of perfection differs from that of the Tiantai school, as will be evident below.

Regarding the division of the three delusions into two bodies: they take passages from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) and arbitrarily divide them into two bodies—the conditioned (*youzuo*) and the unconditioned (*wuzuo*).
Their delusion is even more extreme. Furthermore, the reason the Perfect Teaching does not differentiate [the delusions] is that it harmonizes the provisional (*jia*) and the real (*shi*).

This points out the fallacies of the previous two [positions]: the substance of the former is itself the substance of the perfect [nature], and therefore they cannot be distinguished from one another.

Those [opponents] do not understand this meaning, and thus engage in much groundless discourse. Furthermore, knowing themselves to be ignorant, they say: "However, there is much debate regarding this precept-substance;
it can be understood through the mind and need not be elaborated upon here. One may test the mind by examining its words, and thus the mind may be seen. This is merely a pretext for concealment.

Regarding the "Sacred Texts" (*Shengwen*): the commentaries of our founding masters establish the fundamental tenets and elucidate the essential nature. Their analysis of the textual meaning—what is to be adopted and what is to be discarded—is exhaustive and complete.

Yet these [later followers] have stolen the titles of those commentaries, intermingled them with their own words, and titled them as their own compositions. How can one express the extent of their guilt in concealing the sacred?
Furthermore, there are many more such false assertions among them, though I have merely cited a few examples here. Alas! The times have changed and people have become arrogant; their diligence...

This is called "neglecting study. I desire that the brilliance of the teaching’s core be brought forth to provide a model for future generations; that there be no one in a hundred ages who fails to do so, something I am unable to witness.

Consequently, the ancestral masters’ bequeathed instructions and the ultimate discourse on the precept-substance (*śīla-svabhāva*) were nearly extinguished. Yet, we still rely on the fact that the written records have not fallen into ruin;
they are as clear as the stars and the sun, and as steadfast as jade and gold. Thus, it is by good fortune that I have been able to hear them. For this reason, I have devoted myself...
Based on the commentary and the original record, I have extracted this as a separate work. Because I still regret not having investigated it in detail, I shall briefly state its main points.

First, regarding the two entities of manifest action (*vijñapti*) and non-manifest action (*avijñapti*) across many schools: both names are well known. Second, regarding the established school’s position: manifest precepts take form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) as their essence; this is also well known.
As for non-manifest action taking that which is neither form nor mind as its essence: however, "neither form nor mind" merely serves as a collective category.

The name "Dharma-aggregate" (dharmaskandha) does not actually denote a substantial entity; consequently, throughout the ages, false explanations have proliferated beyond measure. Now, relying on the commentary (*śāstra*), we shall examine its essence through its name.

It is simply a secret discourse on the seeds of goodness (*kuśalabīja*). However, because this minor school did not immediately reveal it directly, it was externally designated as being "neither matter nor mind.
Thus, the commentary states: "Examining its karmic essence, it originally arises from the mind and in turn perfumes [the ālayavijñāna]."
The fundamental mind possesses both capacity and function; even to the point of saying one does not know what its name is, it is forcibly designated as "non-dual.

Examining this text closely, it does not yet speak of "wholesome seeds," but rather says that the mind is perfumed and possesses function. The intended meaning of this esoteric discourse is clearly evident.
One should know that this is precisely the investigation into the essence that is neither matter (*rūpa*) nor mind (*citta*).
Master Zili did not understand this, and thus claimed that the seeds of the four *dharmas* constitute the essence; this disrupts the lineage of our school and is deeply improper. Question:

Since this is discussed cryptically, where is it explicitly revealed? Answer: As in the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) below, how could this not be explicit? Question: Some say that the essence of the four-part precepts is investigated...

"Entering the Mahāyāna"—what is the meaning of this? Answer: Since the teaching of this school is already said to "discuss the essence through partial penetration," how could it be called "probing and entering"?

Therefore, one knows that [the previous interpretation] is incorrect. Regarding the third, the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), there are briefly four sections. First, clarifying the meaning of "perfection":

this refers to harmonizing the preceding schools and precisely pointing to the ultimate reality. The two essences of the preceding schools are, namely, the seeds of goodness (which grasp the fundamental and proceed from the derivative). These seeds of goodness are...

The first two [of the three] bodies (subsuming the branches back into the root) are discussed here according to this perfect teaching (*yuan*). As names are assigned arbitrarily and have no fixed location, the Commentary states:

"Regarding this single dharma, there are three schools of interpretation. Thus, one should know that while there are three modes of differentiation, their essence is in reality non-dual. The rest is as explained below.

Question: If it is said that the essence is only one, yet there are three through conceptual differentiation, then do the first two schools merely possess empty names while ultimately lacking any real substance?
Answer: Although each school maintains its own tenets, how could their essence be contradictory or distinct? It is because they claim it to be different that they forcibly construct other names.
One should know that many schools maintain that the seeds (*bīja*) are form (*rūpa*), whereas the Sautrāntika school maintains that the seeds are neither form nor mind (*citta*). However...

The later Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) points out that the former two [teachings] are merely this. Thus the Commentary says: "Fools claim they are different, and based on this, they give rise to attachments," and so forth.
To express this further through a metaphor: it is like a fine jade in the world; some people, lacking knowledge, mistake the jade for stone, or name it "not-stone."

The essential nature had not yet been revealed; it was only later that someone attained the reality and pointed out the errors of the previous two [positions]. If there were no jade-like essence, how could there be any failure to recognize it?
This serves as a metaphor for the three similar doctrines of the present. Second, regarding the correct naming: various masters of the past have sometimes called it the "Mind-seed" (*cittabīja*).
Some call it "perfuming seeds" (*vāsanā-bīja*). However, perfuming belongs to volitional action (*karma*), whereas the seed is non-volitional (*avijñapti*).
Since we are now referring to the non-volitional, how could there be any confusion between them? Others call it "seeds," but since seeds encompass both good and evil, this too is incorrect.

Here, the name refers specifically to that which takes good seeds as its essence; thus the Commentary states: "It forms good seeds—this is the essence of the precept. (By saying "good," evil is excluded; by not mentioning "volitional perfuming," no confusion arises.)

Question: For what reason is it called the "wholesome seed" (*kuśalabīja*)? Answer: "Wholesome" (*kuśala*) refers to the essential nature of the Dharma (*dharmatā*). "Seed" (*bīja*) is a metaphorical designation.
This means that the sands-of-the-Ganges number of precepts and dharmas are received into the fundamental *ālayavijñāna*, from which they arise continuously as accompanying practices.

These practices are capable of drawing forth future fruits, just as when a grain seed is cast into a field, the sprout emerges, the stalk grows, and the fruit forms upon the ear; the correspondence between cause and effect is without discrepancy. Therefore, it is so named.

Furthermore, regarding the third point, the similarities and differences between the Great and Small Vehicles: Question: Is this [the *Upāsaka-śīla-sūtra*] identical to or different from the essence (*tattva*) of the Bodhisattva precepts?

Answer: The essence is the same, but the conditions (*pratyaya*) are different. As for the difference in conditions: the Great Vehicle involves the three refuges, the four great vows, the invitation of a teacher, the inquiry into prohibitions, the three rounds of *karmavācanā*, and various other ritual procedures;
these are utterly distinct from the two paths of the present Small Vehicle school. As for the identity of essence: it is because the conditions [of the former] serve as...

The auxiliary conditions are external, while the mind is the primary cause. Conditions are remote, whereas the cause is proximate; the essence arises from the cause. Since the preceding [stage] has already produced the superior grade through the mind, we know that the present essence is precisely the Mahāyāna.

Therefore, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, that which is received and maintained through the *jñapti-caturtha-karman* (the formal rite of motion followed by three proclamations) serves to quell worldly censure and suspicion.

It is no different from its nature; it is precisely this same meaning. If that is so, since the bodhisattva precepts described in the sūtras and śāstras take the mental continuum (*citta-santati*) as their essence, and this [mental continuum] is itself the seeds of goodness, why do you say that their essence is the same? Answer: Within those sūtras and śāstras, there are two distinct types of essence:

first, the "essence as such" (*svabhāva-śarīra*), which is the essence of the precepts (*śīla-śarīra*) and is not different from the seeds of goodness mentioned here; second, the "reliant essence" (*āśraya-śarīra*), as explained above.

[The opponent] objects: "The nature of the mind (*cittatā*) is [the essence]. If that is so, then the nature of the mind is merely the basis upon which the substance of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*) relies;

it is not, in reality, the substance of the precepts itself. Therefore, we do not establish it here. Question: "If their substance were identical, how could one distinguish between the various aspects of practice, such as upholding, violating, establishing repentance, and other such forms?

Answer: "Although their substance is considered from the perspective of the ultimate (*pariniṣpanna*), practice must necessarily rely upon formal reception (*samādāna*). Since the reception follows the specific teachings of the respective school, there is no discrepancy in the aspects of practice."
As the commentary states: "The form and status of an ordained bodhisattva are the same as those of the śrāvakas. Furthermore, Śākyamuni Buddha had no separate bodhisattva saṃgha;
the great bodhisattvas entered the śrāvaka saṃgha and followed the sequence of the summer retreat (*varṣā*)—this is precisely the intended meaning.

If this is so, and since the observance or violation of precepts depends on the limits of the specific teaching, why must the determination of their essential substance (*tattva*) necessarily rely on the perfect [teaching]? Answer: Since the essential substances follow many paths, they must be perfectly integrated.

The discipline (*vinaya*) is no different; therefore, one may proceed according to the fundamental tenet. Furthermore, by relying on the teachings to uphold them, one’s reception [of the precepts] accords with their application.

By means of a comprehensive understanding, one causes the mind to be settled within its proper sphere. Once the great understanding has been revealed, even by relying on the minor discipline, one immediately accomplishes the Great Practice.

How could it be necessary to abandon [this practice] before it can be called "great"? Therefore, the Commentary states: "Constantly contemplate this practice; it encompasses the restraint of the precepts (*śīla-saṃvara*) and so forth.
This contains a profound intention that cannot be elaborated upon here. Question: Is this the same as or different from the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*) of Tiantai? Answer:

The principle is the same, yet the explanations differ. What is meant by "the principle is the same"? It is because, in the following commentary, the text cites passages from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and employs the intent of that sūtra to establish this perfect essence (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

However, while that teaching is all-encompassing, this is restricted to a single matter. To bring this into that [teaching], it corresponds to the precept of the noble practices (*śīla-ārya-caryā*) within the wondrous conduct (*praṇidhāna-caryā*) of that sūtra.
What is meant by "the explanations differ"? Here, for the purpose of clarifying the essence of the precepts (*śīla-svabhāva*), one directly takes the Buddha’s...

My intention is to harmonize the two preceding schools and personally arrive at this discourse; it is not that I am adopting their views, but rather that their names and characteristics overlap, and for this reason they differ.

As for the fourth point, establishing the fundamental intent of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao): many [masters] have discussed its essence, and various commentators each rely upon the limitations of their respective teachings.

Mutual calculations differ; yet when one examines the reality and seeks the profound, they ultimately do not constitute the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). However, the Great Sage manifested his traces solely for the sake of one thing:
that which the renunciant harbors in mind is nothing other than the cultivation of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇa*).

If one does not understand this essence of the precepts (*śīla-tattva*), then even if one maintains and guards them with a brilliance like a bright pearl, one will not escape saṃsāra and will sink back into birth and death. Since this matter is profoundly great, my Grandfather [Daosheng]...
The Master, inferring the Buddha’s fundamental intention and exhausting the purpose of his renunciation, transcended into the stage of the Mahāyāna and established this Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

It directly reveals the true substance and reaches the ultimate limit in responding to the capacities of the times. Desiring to cause those who cherish the Way to recognize their original essence and initiate great practice, it allows both ordinary and Hinayana practitioners to bypass lesser paths and directly tread the Great Highway.
The profound secrets of Great Compassion are seen herein. Therefore, in the commentary below, [the Master] extensively...

There is diligent effort; therefore, the practitioner should constantly contemplate this practice, namely the three clusters of precepts (*tri-śikṣā*). By practicing and manifesting them progressively, one ultimately attains the three types of Buddhahood and so forth.

It is further said: "Now that one recognizes these prior conditions, they will ultimately lead to the Mahāyāna; therefore, one must confine the mind within its proper sphere. It is also said: "How could one not contemplate this?
To fail to do so would result in a deficiency in the initial resolve," as explained extensively below. The above summarizes what follows.

Essential. This preface is placed at the beginning so that the wise, upon reading it, may encounter no obstructions in the text. Those who preserve the Way and share the same aspiration must pay deep attention to this.
Truly, it is the essential art for transcending the world and the direct path for cultivation; it is the great matter of one’s entire life—how could one treat it with self-disparagement?
Were it not for the sacred wisdom of our Patriarchs, who could have revealed and manifested it? Moreover, this was after the Patriarchal Teacher had raised it up and proclaimed it.
Gradually flowing down to the present day, this has reached the point of extinction. Consequently, those who study the Vinaya are left bewildered, with no direction to follow;

this is truly a matter of profound sorrow. This [work] thus demolishes past errors and resounds the sacred words once more, providing practical benefit for future generations rather than seeking fame in the present age.
Those among us who understand the Way of our Patriarchs may number only one or two, yet their hearts possess [this realization].

This is a postscript. I earnestly hope that you will cultivate your resolve with vigor and diligence, collaborate in supporting and praising [this work], and fully grasp the profound intent of the Sage. Do not propagate it recklessly.
The Chapter on the Essential Nature of the Precepts (Concluded). The Chapter on the Essential Nature of Observance and Transgression.

Regarding the explanation of the essential nature of the transgressions one commits, it is broadly divided into two parts. First, an account of past traditions; second, the extension of *geyi* (correlative interpretation). The reason for this is as Master Nanshan stated: "If one does not record the errors of the past, one cannot establish the teachings of the present; this is a matter of course. The first part is further divided into three sections: 1. Enhancing the brilliance of the Two Teachings; 2. Subsequently awakening to non-action (*wu zuo*); 3. Harmonizing with the myriad objects of reality. Within the first section: ... [text continues] ... Regarding the first: "The *Sifenlü shanfan buque xingshi chao* (Abridged Commentary on the Practice and Essentials of the Four-Part Vinaya) states: 'In the past, the Great Virtuous Master Daoxuan, relying on the *Vinaya-mātṛkā*, compiled the *Shanfan buque xingshi chao*. He established the ten categories of offenses, which are: 1. The offense of killing sentient beings; 2. The offense of stealing sentient beings; 3. The offense of sexual misconduct regarding sentient beings; 4. The offense of false speech regarding sentient beings; 5. The offense of divisive speech regarding sentient beings; 6. The offense of harsh speech regarding sentient beings; 7. The offense of frivolous speech regarding sentient beings; 8. The offense of taking what is not given regarding insentient things; 9. The offense of sexual misconduct regarding insentient things; 10. The offense of false speech regarding insentient things. This is the first category, the offense of killing sentient beings. It is further divided into two: first, the general explanation of the essence of the offense; second, the specific explanation of the various types of offenses. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'The first category consists of the four grave offenses (*pārājika*) and the thirteen secondary offenses (*saṃghāvaśeṣa*). Among these, the four grave offenses are the most severe. They are: 1. Killing; 2. Stealing; 3. Sexual misconduct; 4. False claims of superhuman powers (*uttarimanuṣya-dharma*). This is the first, the offense of killing. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing human beings; second, the offense of killing non-human beings. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'The first offense of killing refers to humans. There are three grades of humans: superior, middling, and inferior. Superior humans are those who have attained the fruits of the path, such as Stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*) and Arhats. Middling humans are those who have entered the stage of cultivation, such as those practicing the four foundations of mindfulness. Inferior humans are ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*). To kill any of these constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing superior humans. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruits of the path; second, the offense of killing those who have entered the stage of cultivation. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer or an Arhat constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruits of the path. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Arhatship. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of seeing; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of cultivation. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of seeing constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of seeing. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition (*ānantarya-mārga*); second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*). Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of uninterrupted transition constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the form realm. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the four foundations of mindfulness; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the four right efforts. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the four foundations of mindfulness constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the four foundations of mindfulness. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of feelings. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of distraction. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration in the realm of desire; second, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration in the realm of form. Within the first: "The *Xingshi chao* states: 'To kill a Stream-enterer who has attained the fruit through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration in the realm of desire constitutes a grave offense. This is the first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration in the realm of desire. It is further divided into two: first, the offense of killing those who have attained the fruit of Stream-entry through the path of uninterrupted transition in the desire realm by means of the foundation of mindfulness of the body while in the state of meditative concentration in the realm of desire during the preparatory stage (*anāgamya*); second, the offense

Furthermore, there are two [points]. First, the refutation of the distinction between essence (*tattva*) and manifestation (*ākāra*). Second, the formal discussion on the essence of the offenses maintained. Regarding the first:

Zenghui states that for the capacity to maintain or commit [an offense], the mind is the essence and body and speech are the manifestations; for that which is maintained or committed, the dual teachings of prohibition and permission are the essence and the phenomenal facts (*vastu-dharma*) are the manifestations.
Thus, essence and manifestation would be distinct from one another, and their names and meanings would be contradictory. Now, as for "essence," it refers to the substance of a thing...
Regarding the general designation of "essence" (*tǐ*) and "form" (*zhuàng*): form is the appearance of essence. Without form, there would be no way to manifest its essence;
therefore, both essence and form are designated, and name and appearance are revealed together. The object thus manifested is fundamentally without difference: essence itself is form.

The specific characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are themselves the substance (*dravya*). It is like the human body: the four limbs constitute the body. Although one knows its name, one does not yet understand in detail what the characteristics of those four limbs are.
Therefore, one must know that their characteristics consist of the two arms, the two thighs, the bones, blood, skin, and flesh.
Thus, it is known that the substance and the characteristics are one and the same, and cannot be separated. To state it briefly, this refers to what is clarified herein.

A Brief Summary of the Essential Points of the *Vinaya-śāstra* in Ten Sections, composed by the Śramaṇa Yuanzhao of Yuhang.
First, regarding the intention behind the composition, there are two parts: the general and the specific. Within the first, the general intention, there are briefly four points. The first is:
First, to widely expound the holy teachings in order to repay the Buddha’s kindness; second, to fulfill one's original compassionate vows and achieve self-benefit;
third, to rescue and deliver all beings from existence, leading them away from suffering toward the Path; and fourth, to maintain the Three Jewels so they may abide for a long duration.
In both the Flower [Land] and the Fan [Land], whenever the four types of noble and sage dependents undertake any composition, none do so without these reasons; hence it is said that they "pervade."

Furthermore, the following explains the specific intent [of this work]. Briefly, there are four points. First, because the Vinaya Piṭaka is vast and extensive, it is difficult to seek out and comprehend at once.

Thus, the *Jiaoxing zhong* (The Arising of the Teaching) states: "In gathering and guiding, and in providing broad salvation, its ritual applications are truly numerous; what is valued is obtaining its fundamental expositions, yet it is truly difficult to examine its detailed ramifications.

The preface to the *Niseng chao* (Concise Commentary for Nuns) says: "I fear that the Great Text is difficult to penetrate, leading to labor with little efficacy. Furthermore, the *Jieshu* (Commentary on the Precepts)... [text continues].
The preface states: "The original Vinaya is extensive and difficult to seek," and so forth; all of this accords with this intention.

Second, because the accounts transmitted through successive generations were either redundant or incomplete and had not yet been systematized, the intent behind the composition of the *Chao* (Commentary) states: "The works preserved by various masters are characterized by subjective views that are overly verbose and expansive;

I shall now delete and abbreviate them," and the subsequent text says: "Therefore, I immediately supplement what is missing, casting light back upon the nine preceding dynasties. Third, it is for the purpose of making the language concise.

The essential purpose [of this work] is that it be prepared for direct practical application; thus the preface states: "I hope it will be useful when facing critical moments, allowing one to act immediately according to the situation.

It further states: "As one unfolds and reads it, one may rely upon it according to each specific matter. Fourth, its benefit extends to future learners so that they may achieve their goals with little effort and without confusion;
thus the preface states: "It is used to save the labor of those who are newly studying," and as the subsequent text says: "The compiler’s original intent..."
For the sake of beginners, I have not extensively recorded chapters on the meaning and other such details; the rest is not fully transcribed here. The essentials have been set forth as above.
It was because of all these many considerations that this present work came into being.

Second, clarifying the distinctions among the Teachers by way of both sutras and śāstras: the Buddha possesses three bodies (*trikāya*). There are two different traditions, the Mahāyāna and the Hīnayāna.

The Mahāyāna is as described by others; the Hīnayāna is presented in the present treatise. First, that which maintains the noble path is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This, moreover, is of two kinds.

The principle of cessation realized by those of the two vehicles is called the *dharmakāya* of principle. The perfection of the fruit of the fivefold path through cultivation over two or three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* is called the *dharmakāya* of phenomena.
Second, that which is elicited by the accumulation of causes is the *saṃbhogakāya*, also termed the "body born of birth" (*janmakāya*).
This refers to the one who was born in the royal palace, possessed a golden body sixteen feet tall, attained enlightenment at thirty, and proclaimed his parinirvāṇa at eighty.

Third is the transformation body that responds to the capacities of beings; this is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (transformation body) and is also termed the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body). Beginning at the Deer Park, he transformed various non-Buddhists;
these transformations were not limited to one, being adapted to the differing capacities of beings. Thus, as cited by former masters, when the elder Ghoṣila saw [the Buddha]...
