Out of compassion, the preceptor said three times: "Since you have made this request for me to act as your hair-cutting preceptor, you must listen attentively to all my instructions."
5. Parting from One’s Parents and Shedding the Plain Robes.
The Ācārya said: "Those who have left the household life transcend the mundane world and serve as fields of merit for the world; they cannot be treated as subjects by a sovereign."
One who has become a son cannot [simply] remain as such; he ought to receive the respectful offerings of humans and devas.

For this reason, once one has shaved the head and donned the kāṣāya, there is no longer even the propriety of performing formal salutations toward a sovereign or one’s father, let alone toward others. Nevertheless, it was your parents who gave birth to you.

"The kindness of your upbringing is profound; the King who delivered you is likewise of great kindness. You should go to a public place to bid farewell to the King, the ministers, and your parents and kinsmen.
Once this is concluded, return to the dharma-hall so that I may shave your head. Having spoken these words, he immediately rose.

The invoker leads [the practitioner] down from the steps into the courtyard. They burn incense and kneel alternately, reciting the Verses for Parting from Kin (the invoker instructs the practitioner to chant each line following the melody; the verses say):
Wandering through the three realms, one cannot escape the bonds of affection; only by renouncing affection and entering the unconditioned (*asamskrta*) does one truly repay their kindness.

Having finished this verse, he immediately rose. First, facing north, he prostrated to the king (it is not necessary to cry "Ten Thousand Years!"). Next, he prostrated to his parents and kinsmen. (According to the Vinaya...)

However, one must first take leave of one's parents; at this time, it is required by principle that one first pay homage to the king. Having paid homage, one immediately removes the headcloth and crown, dons plain clothing, and puts on the monastic lower robe and short tunic.
Lead the assembly back in until they reach the place of the *ācārya*. They kneel facing one another.

Sixth: Regarding the exhortation to worship the Buddha, the *ācārya* shall then explain the merits of leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*) to inspire joy in them. He should say: "Good son, listen attentively."
Among the six realms of existence, a human body is difficult to obtain; within the human condition, it is difficult to leave the household life.

That you have now been born into the human realm and encountered a Buddha to renounce the world is surely not due to anything other than the profound merit planted in past lives—how else could you have reached this state?

You must establish the mind of renunciation and set the resolve of a true man, vowing to diligently study the Way in order to seek liberation. As the Vinaya Master of the Southern Mountain said: "Truly..."

Truly, those who have left the household life do so because they fear the manifold sufferings of the four enemies, loathe the impermanence of the three realms, bid farewell to the profound affection of their six kin, and renounce their deep attachment to the five desires.

Thus we know that all sentient beings are bound by the four enemies, cling to the three realms, are entangled in their feelings for their six kin, and their minds are addicted to the five desires; it is for this reason that they wander through the cycle of birth and death.

Even after passing through hundreds of thousands of kalpas, undergoing death and rebirth, there will be no way for you to attain liberation. You should abandon all that is false and turn toward the truth.
Uphold the precepts, cultivate meditative concentration, and practice wisdom; perform the six perfections and the myriad practices; study immeasurable dharma-gates.
In the final age, establish the banner of the Dharma, prolong the life of the Buddha, ensure that the Triple Gem remains uninterrupted, and cause all sentient beings to obtain benefit.
If one can act in this way, this is called true renunciation. Such a person may serve as a field of merit for the six realms of existence and provide the seeds for the causes of the three vehicles;
they are worthy of receiving faithful offerings and do not fail the four debts of gratitude. Therefore, the Buddha said:

"If someone were to provide the four requisites of support to Arhats who fill the four continents for a hundred years, it would not equal the merit of someone who, for a single day and night, gives rise to [the thought of...]"

Regarding the merit of renouncing the household life (*pravrajyā*): it is further said that even if one were to erect a stupa made of the seven precious gems reaching as high as the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, its merit would not equal the supreme excellence of the merit of renouncing the household life.
This is explained extensively in the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*), so I shall not cite it here at length.

Having realized that one’s own person is thus so venerable and superior, one should generate even greater reverence and must not allow oneself to regress. (Thus, one should provide such exhortations according to the individual's capacity, describing matters as they arise; it is not necessary to recite these words verbatim. Then, take hold of...
Perform the consecration for him with fragrant water (dropping a small amount onto the crown of his head with the fingers), and recite this verse of praise:
Excellent, O Great Being! You have realized the impermanence of the world; Abandoning the mundane, you have entered Nirvāṇa— A marvel beyond the reach of thought.
(This verse is recited by the ācārya himself in a clear voice. Some have it recited by the invoker; others have the practitioner join in harmony—none of these are correct).
When the verse is finished, he says: "You should go before the Buddha, prostrate to the Buddhas of the ten directions, and recite the verse of taking refuge.
The practitioner then rises and is led before the Buddha. He instructs him, saying:
I take refuge in the Great World-Honored One, Who is able to endure the sufferings of the three realms of existence;
May all sentient beings likewise universally enter the bliss of the unconditioned. (Recite each line according to the rhythm.
7. Shaving the Head and Donning the Robes.
The invoker leads him again to the preceptor (*ācārya*). Approaching and kneeling with their knees crossed, the preceptor wraps a clean cloth around his shoulders and says:
"Shaving off hair and beard is for the sake of abandoning arrogance; donning robes of dyed color is for the sake of removing craving.
In a brief moment, you will be no different from the noble deportment of those of the Three Vehicles; you should rejoice in this yourself. Thereupon, he shaves the four [patches].

[The tonsure master] leaves a small amount of hair at the crown of the head. While the hair is being shaved, the person who has invited [the monastics] recites the *pravrajyā-gāthā* (Verse on Leaving Home):
"Altering one's appearance to maintain the will and integrity, Severing attachment so as to have no kin, Abandoning the household to propagate the Holy Path— May I deliver all people.
(Note: It is also permissible for the entire assembly to recite this together.)
He is then led to the preceptor (*upādhyāya*). As before, they kneel facing each other. The preceptor says, "I shall now shave the crown hair for you.

The practitioner replies, "So be it," and the preceptor proceeds to shave him (or it may also be done while reciting the *pravrajyā-gāthā* once more). Once the shaving is complete, the clean cloth is removed.
The preceptor takes the *kāṣāya* and hands it to the practitioner; the practitioner receives it by placing it upon his head, then returns it to the preceptor. This is repeated three times.
The Upādhyāya personally dressed him and spoke this verse:
"How great is the robe of liberation! The signless field of merit garment. Donning it as one upholds the precepts, One widely delivers all sentient beings.
(This verse was spoken by the Upādhyāya himself; there is no need to respond with a chant.)

8. Instructions on Bestowing the Refuges (From the *Vinaya-śīla-chao*: Once the kashāya has been donned, one should immediately have [the candidate] recite the verses and perform prostrations and scattering of flowers. Nowadays, it is common to bestow the Three Refuges for Turning Away from Heresy;
they are set forth accordingly).

He then proceeded to the preceptor’s quarters and said: "According to the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra*, once the hair has been shaved and the kāṣāya robe has been donned, one subsequently receives the Three Refuges.
When receiving the Five Precepts or the Ten Precepts, each should receive them while ascending the altar. For now, I shall first bestow upon you the Three Refuges that overturn heterodoxy.

This turns away the heterodox mind from beginningless time and causes one to take refuge in the Right Enlightenment of the Triple Gem. You should be shown the realm of the Triple Gem; this is the beginning."

Having entered the gateway of the Way, you are as yet unacquainted with the meaning of the Dharma. For now, I shall point out the Three Jewels for you to dwell in, so that you may have a place to entrust your mind.

You should say: "The sculpted and cast sacred images are the Buddha Jewel; the jade-bound volumes and precious cases are the Dharma Jewel; those who shave their heads, dye their robes, and receive the precepts are the Sangha Jewel.
You should direct your sincere devotion toward them. From this day forward, for as long as this life and body endure, I vow to rely upon the Buddha as my teacher."
"I vow to study the treasury of the Dharma; I vow to become one with the ocean of the Saṃgha. (Having thus provided various exhortations according to their capacities, he says:
"I, [Name], for as long as life lasts, take refuge in the Buddha, take refuge in the Dharma, and take refuge in the Saṃgha" (recited three times). Then, adding the three confirmations, he says:

"I, [Name], having taken refuge in the Buddha for as long as life lasts, having taken refuge in the Dharma for as long as life lasts, and having taken refuge in the Saṃgha for as long as life lasts—thus the Three Refuges are conferred."
Having said this, he addressed him: "Now that you have gone forth, you must rely upon the dharma of those who have gone forth and cultivate the conduct of those who have gone forth.
You must not be indolent or lazy, nor spend your days in aimless idleness. From this day forward, you must first distance yourself from all evils; for now, I shall speak of six kinds."
As for the six kinds [of prohibitions]: first, sexual misconduct; second, theft; third, killing; fourth, lying; fifth, drinking alcohol; and sixth, eating meat.
These six evils are the source that obstructs the Path and the root of saṃsāra; one must distance oneself from them deeply and be careful not to commit them.
One should consult one's preceptor and prepare the three robes and one alms bowl, intending to receive the precepts. These robes and bowl are indeed...
This is the correct ritual of all Buddhas of the three periods of time and the insignia of the noble *śramaṇas*. Even the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist outsiders do not even know its name;
it is only when a Buddha appears in the world that he reveals this unprecedented teaching.

If one does not prepare for it oneself, or if one borrows it at the last moment, according to the clear judgment of the Vinaya, one certainly cannot obtain the precepts. Because one lacks the precepts, one has spent an entire lifetime in vain receiving the offerings of the faithful.
In the future, you will fall into the evil realms and transmigrate through saṃsāra for long kalpas, with no means of liberation. This is no small matter;

you must apply yourself with earnest diligence. Furthermore, you must proactively seek out an enlightened master to inquire about the expedient methods and rituals for receiving the precepts, so that he may provide exhortation and guidance.
To make the mind clear and lucid: ordinary people in this turbid age have weak roots of goodness, and I fear that as they approach receiving the precepts, demonic obstacles may suddenly arise.

From this day forward, you must immediately eliminate all miscellaneous affairs, reciting and upholding [the texts] day and night, praying with sincere devotion for the grace and protection of the Sages.
Upon receiving the precepts, you should either study the Vinaya under a teacher, listen to the sutras, or seek out and investigate [the teachings].

Knowledge. Whether reciting sutras and venerating the Buddha, or engaging in affairs to cultivate merit, one should protect the Buddha-dharma, benefit all sentient beings, refrain from committing evil, and never be indolent.

To seek fame or pursue profit, to defile the ranks of the Sangha, to obscure and destroy the True Dharma, and to instead plant the seeds of suffering—thereby increasing birth and death—is to have no benefit in leaving the household life. Constantly bear this speech in mind for yourself.
Exert yourself with diligence; do not die in vain, lest you later come to regret it (and so forth).
9. Rejoicing and Offering Thanks:
He was led back before the Buddha. Having performed three prostrations and knelt alternately, he was instructed to speak of his rejoicing. The verse says:
"How fortunate to encounter a Buddha! Who would not rejoice? May my merit and vows coincide with this moment;
I have now obtained the benefit of the Dharma. (Recite each line as it is spoken.

Having finished speaking, he again prostrates before the assembly and his two teachers. Then, he instructs the monks present to descend and sit, so that he may receive the salutations of his six types of relatives.
Congratulations. Rejoice in their aspiration for the Way (if one fears the proceedings will become too protracted, it is also permissible to offer congratulations after the assembly has dispersed).
Ten: Prayers of Dedication and Transference of Merit (this section does not exist in the Vinaya; it is a contemporary practice).
Whether it be the *upādhyāya*, the *ācārya*, the person who has been invited, or the standard ritual proclaimer (*pratideśaka*) used by the monastery, any of these may perform the role.
One should hold the hand-incense burner (*pāṇi-bhoga*), offer incense, and once the *karmadāna* has struck the mallet once, he says:
All the merit derived from the dharmas practiced above is offered as a blessing to Brahmā, Śakra, and the Four Heavenly Kings; to the eight classes of devas, nāgas, and others;
to the true lords of the *gārāma* temples; and to the numinous and wise deities of the local soil. May each stir their majestic spiritual power to stabilize the mind and protect the Dharma.
May the present Emperor’s sacred transformation be inexhaustible; may the civil and military officials dwell forever in their ranks and positions;

and may the monastics, parents, virtuous and non-virtuous spiritual friends, the faithful offerings from the ten directions, and all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm, by virtue of these roots of goodness, together ascend to the other shore.
Recite the name of Śākyamuni Buddha. Strike the mallet according to the ritual sequence. Upon completing the recitation, perform the "Verse for the World" (*chuzu shijie bai*).

Then, disperse to offer congratulations and so forth (or recite the text for "Inviting and Offering Blessings to the Devas, Nāgas, and the Eight Divisions of the Higher Realms," which appears in the *Zhizhe Fahua Chan Yi*; this may be used as a model.
Nowadays, many recite rhymed prose, which entirely misses the intent of dedication and auspicious praise; all such instances should now be corrected and not allowed to conform to vulgar customs).

*Shoujie fangbian shamen* (The Śramaṇa on the Expedient Means for Receiving Precepts), by Yuanzhao. In the third year of the Yuánfēng era, he produced the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* for the sake of various śrāmaṇeras, stating:
"Whenever one wishes to receive the precepts, one must first preach the Dharma to them, guiding and instructing them so that they may attain understanding. Regarding this single [point]...
By giving rise to a mind of loving-kindness and compassion toward all objects of perception, one attains the superior precepts (*adhiśīla*).
Therefore, it is known that one must possess clear understanding through wisdom before proceeding to receive them. Now, for the sake of the six stages, they shall be explained in sequence.
First, clarifying the essence of the dharma received (identifying the mind’s aspiration for reception; one must recognize which dharma it is).

Now, desiring to receive the precepts, what precepts are being received? What are the characteristics of these precepts? It refers to the dharma of the precepts established by the Buddha when he appeared in the world.
To restrain body and speech and to subdue the activities of the mind, there are many kinds of precepts. One must first receive the five precepts and the ten precepts;
that which is received now is the full ordination (*upasampadā*) of a great *bhikṣu*. According to the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra*, these number two hundred and fifty;
briefly stated, they are eighty-four thousand; extensively, they are immeasurable and boundless. They are the [teachings] of the Buddhas of the ten directions and the Three Vehicles.
Because the worthy and the sages practice this together, it is called the "Noble Dharma" (*āryadharma*).

Now, having resolved to receive this dharma, one must perform the ritual before the seats of the ten masters atop the actual altar; thus, causes and conditions will harmonize and the mind and its objects will merge in stillness.

The unconditioned (avijñapti) arises and is received within the mind; this is termed the "precept-substance" (śīla-tattva). Having attained this dharma, one maintains and honors it for the rest of one's life, guarding it as if it were a bright pearl.
It is called a "noble field of merit" (puṇyakṣetra); it is the true Jewel of the Saṃgha, which perpetuates the lineage of the Buddhas and raises high the banner of the Dharma.
Therefore, one should know that at the time of receiving [the precepts], one must apply oneself with even greater care; the great matter of a single lifetime must not be taken lightly.
Second, explaining the conditions for the recipient (having already understood the dharma of the precepts, one knows that receiving them necessarily relies upon these conditions).
First, one must be of the human realm; for those in the heavens, asuras, hells, hungry ghosts, and animals cannot receive it.
Second, one must have all faculties complete; those who are insane, mute, deaf, or physically deformed also cannot receive it. Third, one must have a pure physical vessel;
those who have previously violated the Buddha’s precepts or committed grave evil deeds also cannot receive it. Fourth, one must possess the marks of a renunciant. One must...

Shaving the hair and donning the *kāṣāya*—if one wears the robes of an outsider (*tīrthika*) or secular clothing, it is not called receiving full ordination (*upasaṃpadā*). Fifth, the method for obtaining a portion [of the precepts]:
this requires first receiving the ten precepts of a *śrāmaṇera*. Furthermore, one must early on prepare the three robes (*tricīvara*) and one alms bowl (*pātra*), which may not be borrowed.

When one’s age is complete, one first requests the three masters (*ācārya*) and seven witnesses; only then does one beg for the precepts from the Saṃgha. If even one condition is deficient, the dharma [is not fulfilled].
Thus it is not established.
Third, clarifying the scope of the objects for generating the precepts (although all conditions must be present, one must clarify that the objects are universal).

Although the objects of these conditions are numerous, they do not exceed two types: first, sentient objects, namely the sands of Ganges-rivers of beings throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time.

Buddhas, as well as bodhisattvas, pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, devas, humans, asuras, hell-beings, hungry ghosts, and animals—down to mosquitoes, gadflies, bugs, lice, and the most minute crawling creatures;

those beyond the six realms of existence, including beings in the intermediate state (*antarābhava*)—all such classes of beings, pervading the ten directions and spanning the three periods of time, are immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable. All of them...

Second, the non-sentient realm: this refers to all the minute particles of the world, the lands, mountains, rivers, the great earth, grasses, trees, flowers, and fruits—even down to a single flower, a single leaf, a single object, or a single particle. According to their respective quantities, one likewise generates the precepts for each.
This extends even to the two truths of emptiness and existence, the principle of cessation and nirvana, the sacred teachings and scriptures, as well as images and stupas.

The temples, earth, water, fire, wind, space, consciousness, and so forth—in short, the two types of retribution, the environment and its inhabitants, throughout the entire great trichiliocosm, are all objects of the precepts.
Why is this? Because prior to receiving them, one’s transgressions were created according to the mind, pervading the entire dharma-realm.

Now, desiring to advance and receive the precepts, one reverses those former evil objects and gives rise to wholesome thoughts; therefore, the cause from which the precepts arise likewise pervades [the entire realm].
The Dharma-realm, which contains the essence of the precepts, is likewise boundless; know it thus.

Fourth, clarifying the arousal of the mind based on the objective realm (the *Lüchāo* explains three grades of mind; the middle and lower grades result in the attainment of the precepts but are not superior.
Now one must directly seek the superior grade, and therefore this is explained in detail).

Having understood the measure of the objective realm, one should know how to resolve the mind [for awakening], speaking these words: "I, [Name], reflect that since beginningless time, I have lost my original nature.

Following sensory objects and stirring with discursive thoughts, I have committed manifold evil karmas and undergone the suffering of birth and death, sinking and drifting through long kalpas without hope of liberation.
Relying on past conditions, I have been born into the human realm; having encountered the Buddha and left the household life, I am about to receive the purification..."

Regarding the precepts: I now resolve my mind and establish three vows. From this day forth, for as long as this present body lasts, I vow to sever all evil, I vow to cultivate all goodness, and I vow to deliver all sentient beings.

This is for the sake of accomplishing the three clusters of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣā-saṃvara*), for the sake of proceeding toward the three gates of liberation, and specifically for the sake of seeking the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood, which is Great Nirvāṇa. Furthermore...

By means of this Dharma, he guides sentient beings, causing them to reach nirvana and ensuring that the Dharma endures for a long time. (The words are concise while the matters are extensive; the following is a brief explanation.)
The commentary explains: "All evils" refers to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, lying, greed, anger, and wrong views; all bodily and verbal actions that are contrary to the Dharma;
and even the afflictions, ignorance, fetters, and entanglements within the three realms.

"All virtues" refers to the mundane meritorious practices of humans and devas, as well as the supramundane paths of the Three Vehicles and the practices for realizing the fruit of Buddhahood. [This applies to] all sentient beings.

Those who have not yet realized the fruit of the Way—comprising all sentient beings across the good and evil realms, totaling ten thousand types to be liberated—the threefold aggregate of precepts (*tri-śīla-saṃgraha*) is the Dharma of the Bodhisattva:

(1) the precept of restraining misconduct (*saṃvara-śīla*), (2) the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*), and (3) the precept of benefiting sentient beings (*sattva-artha-kriyā-śīla*). The three gates of liberation (*trīṇi vimokṣa-mukhāni*) are the wisdom of contemplation for entering the Path:

(1) the gate of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa-mukha*), (2) the gate of signlessness (*animitta-vimokṣa-mukha*), and (3) the gate of wishlessness (*apraṇihita-vimokṣa-mukha*). The fruit of *nirvāṇa* is the fruit of Buddhahood as the three bodies (*trikāya*).

[The three bodies are: (1) the Dharmakāya, (2) the Sambhogakāya, and (3) the Nirmāṇakāya). "Guiding sentient beings" refers to the practice of benefiting others. (The above lists the names in general; the following provides specific correlations and explanations.)
First, the restraint of discipline prohibits evil; because it severs evil, it comprises the *saṃvara-śīla* (precept of restraint).

Furthermore, by contemplating that all evils are merely transformations of the mind, and that their nature and characteristics are equal—being without action and without recipient—one is able to advance toward the gate of liberation through non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣamukha*).
When deluded attachments have ceased, the essence of the true mind is revealed; this is called the Dharma-body Buddha, which constitutes the perfection of the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).
Second, because one cultivates wholesome deeds, merit and wisdom proceed together; this is the precept of gathering wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla*).

Furthermore, by observing that all wholesome phenomena arise from various conditions and that no substantial reality can be found within them, one is able to incline toward the gate of liberation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vimokṣamukha*) and realize that all phenomena are signless (*animitta*). Thus, one passes through...
Having diligently practiced throughout kalpas and perfected all virtues, he is called the Sambhogakāya Buddha; this constitutes the fulfillment of wisdom and merit.

Third, because he delivers sentient beings, he gathers all things through compassion; this is the precept of gathering in sentient beings. Furthermore, as he traverses countless lands within the dust-motes of the universe, employing innumerable skillful means to teach and transform beings, yet fully understands that the phenomena of transformation are like illusions and dreams, he is able to advance toward signless liberation.

The Gate: Responding to conditions and manifesting according to the capacity of beings to uproot suffering and bestow happiness—like the moon reflected in water, appearing according to the size of the vessel—is called the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha (the Body of Response).
This constitutes the perfection of the virtue of beneficence (*anuśaṃsā*). Thus far, we have discussed the three clusters, the three liberations, the three Buddhas, and the three virtues.

These are all accomplished by means of the aforementioned three vows. Therefore, one should know that these three vows are the causal seeds of the three bodies (*trikāya*). Furthermore, these three bodies are the very essence of my own mind.
Enveloped by delusion since beginningless time, false movement gave rise to karma, and thus one undergoes the cycle of rebirth.

Failing to realize that all karmas originate from one's own mind and flow and transform according to conditions, one now understands their falsity and turns toward the reality; therefore, one receives the pure precepts, vowing to uphold them with steadfast resolve.

This is precisely the very beginning of setting forth on the quest for the Buddha’s Bodhi; it is called the "superior grade of the resolute mind" (*adhimātra-citta*), which certainly brings about the arousal of the superior grade of precepts (*adhimātra-śīla*).
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The precepts are the foundation of unsurpassed Bodhi; one should fully maintain the pure precepts. Furthermore, a verse from the Vinaya states:
"In this way, O sons of the Buddha, diligently seek the foundation of the prohibitive precepts; never turn your face toward what is heterodox."
Flowing [into saṃsāra], they drown in the ocean of birth and death; this is the clear evidence.
Fifth, clarifying the application of the mind in reverent upholding (the correspondence between mind and object, internalizing the essential core).
Before reaching the altar, one generates the aspiration for enlightenment before the Buddha image as described above; upon ascending the altar, one’s joy and celebration redouble.
One wonders what roots of goodness from past lives have brought one to encounter such a supreme condition. One should contemplate the Master as being identical to the Buddhas of the ten directions:
"This body of mine is now delivered through another; the pure dharma of the precepts is received from another; the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body is sustained by another."

Success is attained. At the time of the formal ritual (*karmavācanā*), one should concentrate the mind and direct one's thoughts to universally encompass the aforementioned sentient and non-sentient objects.
Because these objects are vast, the mind likewise pervades them, remaining present in every thought-moment without becoming distracted or scattered.

One should visualize one’s own body as being coextensive with the entire realm of empty space, capable of containing the dharma-realm of infinite, fine-grained precepts. At this juncture, one must apply oneself with profound care; do not allow the mind to wander.
Regarding other matters: if one errs by even a hair’s breadth, one will merely be stained by the flow of the Dharma and waste an entire lifetime in vain. How can one not be cautious? Sixth:

Questioning the gravity of obstacles versus their lightness (*律鈔* states: "When [the candidate] is a *śrāmaṇera*, instruct him to list his name, manifest the number [of precepts], and recite them so that he recognizes their characteristics.
If he does not clearly recognize them, the reception of the precepts is not accomplished").

First: Have you not committed a pārājika offense? (Answer: No. This refers to one who, having previously received the Buddha’s precepts, has committed one of the four grave offenses; thus, they are like a person caught at the edge of the Buddha-ocean, named after this metaphor.
Second: While you were a layperson, have you not defiled a pure-precepted bhikṣuṇī? (Answer: No. Third:

While you were a layperson or a śrāmaṇera, have you not eavesdropped on others reciting the precepts or performing karmavācanā, falsely representing yourself as a bhikṣu? (Answer: No. This refers to a layperson or...)

[He remains] for a long time (this refers to eavesdropping on the *poṣadha* and *karmavācanā* rituals of the Great Saṃgha). Fourth: "Have you never been a follower of external paths (*tīrthika*), who, after coming to receive the precepts, returned to being a follower of external paths?

Are you now coming back [to receive them again]? [Answer: "No. (This means that one who previously abandoned external paths to come and receive the Buddha’s precepts, but later returned to heterodoxy, is required to come again to receive them.

Fifth: "Are you not one of the five kinds of *paṇḍaka* (eunuchs)? [Answer: "No. (There are five types: 1. those born so; 2. those made so by surgery—that is, those whose sexual organs were removed with a blade; 3. those whose lust arises from jealousy upon seeing another engage in sexual intercourse; 4. those who suddenly undergo a transformation.)

For five half-months he was capable of sexual intercourse, and for [the remaining] five half-months he was not. Sixth: "Have you not killed your father? [He replied: "No. Next, up to the tenth, these are the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
Seventh: "Have you not killed your mother? [He replied: "No. Eighth: "Have you not killed an Arhat? [He replied: "No. Ninth: "Have you not caused a schism in the Saṃgha? [He replied: "No.

(This refers to establishing false Triple Gems, destroying the Buddha’s True Dharma, and causing the Saṃgha to hold divergent views so that they no longer obtain the benefits of the Path. Tenth: "Have you not, with an evil mind, shed the blood of a Buddha? [He replied: "No."

[Question: Is it not [the case that] one’s own blood [cannot be offered]? (Answer: No. Regarding the two preceding difficulties: they existed during the Buddha’s lifetime, but do not exist in the final age. Eleventh:
Are you not a son of a *deva* or a son of an *asura*, but rather a "non-human" (*amanuṣya*) who has transformed into human form to come and receive the precepts? (Answer: No. Twelfth:

Regarding its end: this refers to turning the mind toward the Pure Land and making a firm vow to be reborn there.

then birth [in that realm] will be assured. Why harbor further doubt? Sentient beings in the末法 (mofa) age have deeply heavy delusions and karma, and thus they doubt themselves.

yet, upon encountering a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who instructs them to recite the ten recitations (*daśanāman*), they still attain rebirth in the Pure Land. How much more so for those who practice pure karma throughout their entire lives—what cause for doubt could there be?

He was born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī). As a State Preceptor and Head of the Sangha, he followed in the footsteps of the Tathāgata; renouncing his royal throne, he became a bhikṣu.

Thus we know that the primary purpose of leaving the household life is to renounce wealth and status, sever ties of affection, maintain few desires and non-action, and single-mindedly honor the work of the Path.
I have recently heard that the Sangha Superintendent has already fashioned the three cotton robes, which are the identifying marks of all Buddhas.
This is the formal ordination of one who has left the household life. I vow that in the future I shall return to my native land, uphold the precepts, and cause the Three Jewels to flourish.

Because the sixteen sublime contemplations (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā*) integrate the methods of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, there has arisen a dispute between "contemplating the mind" and "contemplating the Buddha.

This is merely a proliferation regarding whether one contemplates the mind or the Buddha. Upon examining the various Mahāyāna contemplation methods, although the contemplating mind is one and the same, the objects contemplated differ according to the capacity of the practitioner.
Furthermore, two types are taught: first, taking the mind itself as the object of contemplation, as in the *Tiantai Zhiguan*.

The *Guanxin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind), the *Xianshou fajie guan* (Contemplation of the Dharmadhātu by the Worthy Head), the *Huanguan* (Contemplation of Returning to the Source), the *Nanshan jingxin guan* (Contemplation of Purifying the Mind at Mount Nanshan), and even the "wall-contemplation" of the Shaolin [monks], all point to the essential nature of the presently manifest awakened mind as the Pure Land.

As in the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, where it is said that "the mind being pure, the land is pure," in the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*, both the hells and celestial palaces are all considered pure lands. Master Zhi and the Sixth Patriarch, among others, all stated: "This very mind is purity."
As for "the land," there is no need to seek it in the West or elsewhere. This refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*) as the land, which is inhabited by the Buddha alone.
Although sentient beings do not depart from it, they have yet to manifest perfect enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*).

The contemplative methods elucidated in various Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* and the *Sūtra on the Examination of Karma* are all methods of contemplating the principle of non-arising (*anutpāda*) for the purpose of destroying delusions and entering the Path within this very realm. Second, regarding the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas...

In the practice of *sādhana*, one takes the physical forms of the primary and secondary marks (*laksana* and *vyañjana*) as the object of contemplation, as seen in the *Buddhākṣepaṇasamudra-sūtra*, the *Samantabhadra-caryā-prasthāna-sūtra*, the *Maitreya-sūtra on the Upper Rebirth*, the *Amitāyurdhyāna-sūtra*, and others.

The titles of these texts clearly designate the distinction between the subject and the object. Furthermore, there are three specific categories: first, the *Buddhākṣepaṇasamudra-sūtra* concerns the contemplation of Śākyamuni; the *Samantabhadra-* [text]...
First, the *Bhadra-caryā-praṇidhāna Sūtra* involves contemplating Samantabhadra; one contemplates him without ever departing from this realm.
This is also for the purpose of shattering hindrances, extinguishing transgressions, and assisting the realization of the contemplation of principle (*li-guan*), rather than seeking rebirth.

Second, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* involves using the mind to contemplate the celestial realm of Maitreya’s Inner Court, seeking rebirth in that heaven (these two do not transcend the Sahā world). Third, the *Sūtra on Contemplating the Buddha of Immeasurable Life*.

The sixteen kinds of contemplation all involve directing one’s thoughts beyond ten trillion lands to the west toward the adornments of the primary and secondary aspects of Amitābha’s Pure Land, seeking rebirth therein.

The setting sun is suspended like a drum, serving as a signpost for the direction of sending forth one's thoughts; how could this not be a clear scriptural authority?

Moreover, the statement that one "gathers up that environment and its inhabitants and returns to contemplate them with the mind" arises from a failure to discern [the distinction between these two].

Alas! How many people have been led astray? Whenever I think of this, I cannot help but shed tears. Since the commentaries and sub-commentaries of the various masters have circulated in the world, many who study the teachings have failed to attain birth in the Pure Land.

Yet, there are many who, though they are laymen or laywomen (gyō-ō and gyō-ba) ignorant of the characteristics of the teachings (*kyō-sō*), believe directly [in rebirth] and are born [as humans].

If this were so, would the Sixteen Contemplations not be contemplations of principle (*ri-kwan*)? Why, then, does the Commentary explain them using the Three Contemplations (*san-kwan*)? Answer: It is not meant that contemplations of principle consist solely of contemplating the mind (*kan-shin*).
If one penetrates the principle, then the dharmas of the Buddha, the dharmas of sentient beings, and the dharmas of the mind are all the principle itself. Therefore it is said:

The Genealogical Record of the Patriarchs of the Nanshan Vinaya School:
The Founder, Venerable Dharmatrāta,
was a disciple of Kumāralāta and the master of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, which is the school followed by Nanshan.
The Second Patriarch, Venerable Dharmagupta, was originally a monk from Western India; he initially relied upon the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* when conferring the precepts upon others.
The Third Patriarch was Vinaya Master Fachong of Beitaishan.
Our school primarily studies the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, yet we have examined the formal reception of the precepts and found that the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* was first transmitted [to China].
The Fourth Patriarch, Daocuo— the Vinaya Master Fuli, a disciple of Daocheng—
was the first to compose the *Yi* (Explanations of Doubts), providing a systematic analysis and commentary on the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.
The Fifth Patriarch, Dajue Hui Guang Vinaya Master,
received the Vinaya from Fu and composed ten fascicles of commentary, widely opening the doors and windows [of the teaching].
The Sixth Patriarch was Gao Qi Daoyun Vinaya Master.
Shengling Guangshi also composed a sub-commentary (*chao-shu*) to analyze and explain the extensive text.
The Seventh Patriarch, Master Hong of Hedao in Hebei,
received the teachings from Master Yun and likewise possessed a Vinaya commentary (*lü-shu*), though its number of fascicles remains undetermined.
The Eighth Patriarch was Master Hongfu Zhishou, a disciple of Master Hong;
his commentaries comprise twenty fascicles and comprehensively penetrate all schools of thought.
The Ninth Patriarch was Master Nanshan Chengzhao.
The primary masters from whom [the lineage] was received have produced extensive writings that circulate in the world today.

The original manuscript was lost. In the fourth year of the Zhizhong era, it was returned from that country. Originally there were three fascicles;

now we have only obtained the first and middle fascicles, while the final fascicle has not yet been seen. Recent scholars divided the middle fascicle into a "lower" one merely to maintain the traditional number of fascicles, thereby losing the original structure.
Now, these two fascicles have been expanded into four, as they are currently circulated.

The *Sifen lü shanbu suiji jiemó* (Abridged and Supplemented Manual of Karmavācanā for the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya) in two fascicles was produced in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era and revised in the twenty-first year. Originally it consisted of one fascicle, later divided into three.
It is extant in the Tripitaka.

The *Suiji Jiemoshu* (Commentary on the *Sifenlü Shanchu Suiji Jiemochao*), in four fascicles, was composed in the ninth year of the Zhenguan era and revised in the twenty-second year. Originally consisting of two fascicles, it was later expanded to four.
It is now divided into eight fascicles. The currently circulating *Sifenlü hanzhù jìběn* (The Four-Part Vinaya Containing Annotated Prātimokṣa) consists of two fascicles;
it was first produced in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era and re-edited in the second year of the Yonghui era. Originally it was one fascicle, but it was later expanded into two. Now...
It is divided into three fascicles. Regarding the *Jiexiben shu* (Commentary on the Essential Text of the Precepts) of the *Sifenlü* (Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), it consists of four fascicles;

it was composed in the eighth year of the Zhenguan era and revised in the second year of the Yonghui era. Originally it was in three fascicles, but later became four fascicles. [This is] the current version.
It is divided into eight fascicles and is currently in circulation.

*The Monastic Code of Precepts Compiled from the Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Sifenlü shanding sengjieben), one fascicle, was produced in the second month of winter in the twenty-first year of the Zhenguan era. Its wording was revised and finalized so that it might be fully recited and practiced by the world; it remains in use today.
It was widely circulated.
The *Sifenlü biquni chao* (Abridged Commentary on the Bhikṣuṇī Vinaya of the Four-Part School) in three fascicles does not appear in various catalogs;
it is now included based on its later circulation. Its title states it was composed in the nineteenth year of the Zhenguan era. It is now divided [into sections].
Six fascicles. Currently extant.
*Commentary on the Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa* of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, two fascicles;
produced during the Zhenguan era. Originally one fascicle, later divided into two; not yet seen.
The *Sifenlü shanding niji ben* (Abridged Bhikṣuṇī Prātimokṣa of the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya), one fascicle;
issued in the second year of the Yonghui era. Currently in circulation.
The *Liangchu qingzhong yi* (Ritual for Judging the Gravity of Offenses), one fascicle.

There is a work titled *The Ritual for the Measurement and Weight of Vestments* (*Chuliang qingzhong yi*). It was composed in the eleventh year of the Zhenguan era and revised in the second year of the Qianfeng era;
it is currently in circulation. One fascicle: *The Ritual for the Robes and Vestments of the Śramaṇa Community* (*Shimen zhangfu yi*).
Compiled in the fourth year of the Xianqing era (659). Revised in this same year. Currently in circulation.

Although this is not exclusively a Vinaya text, it was originally intended for the monastic community; therefore, it is included here.

One fascicle of the *Preface to the Propagation of the Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
At the beginning of the scripture,

The *Zhujing yaoji* (Essential Collection from Various Sutras) consists of twenty fascicles.
In the current canon, the title states it was compiled by Xuanyun; however, the *Suixian yin* (Phonetic Index of the Case-Contents) states it was compiled by Daoshi.

Furthermore, some claim it was "compiled by Dao" or "translated by Dao," all of which are errors. Now, based on the preface at the beginning of the volume, the Master himself states: "I once, during the Xianqing..."

I read through all the sutras, selecting the essentials according to their practical value for those capable of practicing them. The karmic retributions of good and evil deeds are set forth here in systematic detail.
These thirty chapters are bound into two volumes, hoping that both monastics and laypeople will rely upon and practice them.
Thus, it is evident that this is not the work of another, as it is now seen in the Great Canon.

*Jiàn dàzàng jiéjí zhèngjiào zhùchí yífǎ yí* (Ritual for Seeing the Great Canon, Compiling the Orthodox Teachings, and Upholding the Bequeathed Dharma), six fascicles;

Compiled on the eighteenth day of the ninth month in the second year of the Lín-dé era at Xìmíng-sì. It is also called *Shìshì-pǔ* (Genealogy of the Śākya Clan);

It is followed by the *Hou ji gaoseng zhuan* (Sequel to the Biographies of Eminent Monks) in ten fascicles.

also called *Yaolu* (Essential Records); some say it is in two fascicles, but this has not been seen.

One fascicle of the *Tújīng* (Illustrated Scripture), compiled in the second year of the Qiánfēng era; not seen. Because it was previously attached to the preceding work, the characters "Zhīhuán" (Sanghārāma) have been omitted here.

Compiled at Linggan Monastery in the second year of the Qianfeng era [667 CE]. Currently extant.

Not seen. The collected works of Grand Master Yuan of Mount Lu in eleven fascicles— or,
according to some accounts, ten fascicles— are not yet seen.

Not seen. The *Ximing si lu* (Record of Ximing Monastery) in three fascicles was compiled in the fourth year of the Xianqing era; not seen.

The five categories above comprise a total of fifty-seven items, amounting to two hundred and sixty-seven fascicles.
If calculated by small fascicles, they total two hundred and ninety fascicles. Furthermore, the catalogs of various schools differ from one another. Among them—
The *Dianlu* lists eighteen sections comprising one hundred and fourteen fascicles; the *Kaiyuan lu* lists eight sections comprising eighty-one fascicles;
and the current *Zanglu* lists nine sections comprising one hundred and four fascicles. For now, we shall rely on what is currently extant.
As recorded above, the remainder shall await future continuation.
Since the Buddhist teachings reached this land from the Later Han through the Cao Wei dynasty, only two hundred years had passed. As for those who were transformed by them:

They merely adopted the practice of shaving the hair as a departure from local custom; however, they had never received the formal precepts. It was not until the Jiaping era that Dharmakāla arrived from Western India to propagate the Dharma in the capitals of Jing and Luo.
He began to establish the orthodox tradition of study according to the Dharma, instituting the conferral of the full precepts upon ten monks.

He subsequently produced the *Sengqi jieben* (Mahāsāṃghika Vinaya) and the *Jixin* (Precept Heart), which he used to support the practical application of the rules. These are what the Patriarchs refer to as the Vinaya of the Eastern Land.
This was the precedent. By the time of the Yao Qin dynasty, the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations) was first translated.
Since the true teaching had only just begun to emerge and its origins and lineages were not yet distinguished, those companions who practiced the precepts accepted it for immediate use.

Thus, they adopted the *Caturvargika-vinaya* as their core body, recited the *Prātimokṣa-sūtra* of the *Mahāsāṃghika*, and followed the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* as the basis for their conduct. The confusion regarding the schools of the Vinaya began from this point. Thus it is said.

Subsequently, the *Dharmaguptaka*, *Mahāsāṃghika*, and *Mahīśāsaka* Vinayas were translated in succession. Because the precepts (Prātimokṣa) previously produced by them corresponded perfectly in their definitions and characteristics, the *Mahāsāṃghika* alone flourished during that era.
Later, reaching the Northern Wei dynasty, Master Tanyao investigated the sources and scrutinized the fundamentals.

Distinguishing the essential nature from the practical application, he subsequently ceased his previous studies and first lectured on the *Sifen lü* (Four-Part Vinaya). Dao Fu and others followed him, and commentaries (*zhangshu*) emerged therefrom.

Since then, the eminent masters who have transmitted and practiced this tradition have appeared in succession without fail. Nevertheless, various schools remained in conflict, with proponents of the provisional and the real vying for dominance;

the two traditions of transformation (*hua*) and regulation (*zhi*) were intermingled and undifferentiated. Master Shou [Daoxuan] unraveled the lineage of these schools, and although they were distinguished, their practical implementation...
Their strategic plans and deliberations were likewise not yet fully detailed or comprehensive.

It was not until the time of Master Nanshan, who appeared between the Sui and Tang dynasties, that these matters were perfected. He extensively investigated the various schools of thought and uniquely mastered the study of the precepts.

He examined the grand regulations of the Sages to their ultimate limit and followed the traces left by Dharmamitra. Looking back upon the ancient statutes with discernment, he felt deep compassion for later students. From this...

This work was composed and brought forth. Generally speaking, the attainment of the intended meaning lies in the practice of the teachings; therefore, the *Shishi Yaolüe Shichao* (Essentials of the Vinaya) is presented first.

It unifies the four Piṭakas and encompasses the two vehicles, distinguishing between different schools and investigating various doctrines. It is truly the grand framework that sustains the tradition and the level path for those seeking liberation.
Following this is the *Shiyi Chao* (Collection of Essential Meanings), which gathers the secret essentials of the Vinaya. Then there is the *Jieye Suo* (Commentary on Precepts and Karma).

By unfolding and detailing these hair-like points of the system, one is able to receive its teachings regarding the characteristics of the body [of precepts], the gravity or lightness of upholding or violating them, the ritual procedures for the assembly and the individual, and the methods for governing the mind and cultivating the person; thus, the daily practices are fully encompassed.

Therefore, for all who enter our gate, although their specific studies differ, they daily receive its benefits beyond description. Is this not like a wall several *zhang* high, through which those who find the door gain entry?
It was rare indeed. When the heavens sent down rain, did all things not give thanks to Heaven? From that time on, the works of the various masters of the nine dynasties were as if unheard of.
Yet, for several hundred years following his passing, [his teachings] poured forth uncontrollably.

Were it not for the Great Being of the Four Reliances who manifested them during this age of semblance, who else could have brought it to such a state? Aside from these, there are also commentaries, annotations, biographies, ritual compendiums, and diagrams.
Record. Some works elucidate their own schools’ tenets, while others provide commentaries on the sūtras and śāstras; their volumes are so numerous that they cannot be easily enumerated.

However, due to the vast distances between regions and the long intervals between eras—furthermore, following the calamities of the Huichang persecution and the chaos of the Five Dynasties—the scriptures of most schools were reduced to ashes.
Consequently, more than half of the ancestral masters’ teachings have been lost or scattered. Moreover, as for the teaching...
Thus, writing serves to distinguish the Way, and the literary record serves to sustain the teaching. If the literary record should fall into ruin, the teaching will not endure;
if the teaching does not endure, the Way will not be clarified. Therefore, as for literature in this world, how could it be discarded?

For this reason, in the past, those who revered the Way and assisted the teaching, concerned that these writings were about to perish, have often compiled the names of various masters and assembled them into separate records.
This work enables those who come to it to find its names and obtain its source; what it enumerates is already extensive.
However, the compilation is not yet thorough; there are chronological errors, and the arrangement is disordered and confused, making it insufficient for consultation.

Now, based on the Buddhist scriptures, the *Kaiyuan Shijiao Lu* and other catalogs, as well as various texts such as the commentaries on the precepts and their postscripts, I have annotated, examined, compared, and cross-referenced them to recompile this single volume. Each [entry]...

Categorized according to their respective types, they are divided into five sections. As for those who distance themselves from evil and purify the roots of bodily conduct—the very foundation of the Path—nothing is greater than the Vinaya;
therefore, it comes first. As for exhausting the spirit and dispelling worldly burdens, nothing is more profound than the Sūtras and Śāstras; therefore, it follows next.
To maintain what is precarious and to resist insults must depend upon extensive protection; thus there is the third [category].

To be diligent and self-advancing must rely upon proper measures and methods; thus there is the fourth. For illustrious traces to shine far and wide must depend upon transmission and recording; thus there is the fifth.
As for the opening and closing of the fascicles, the chronological sequence of the years, whether they are currently in circulation or have been lost, and whether they have been compiled into...

The Great Canon contains various titles for this work, all of which are fully recorded in the annotations. Nevertheless, despite my own shortcomings and lack of refinement, I have ventured to append this preface at the end, hoping that readers may thereby gain a general understanding of our school’s essential principles.

In the third year of Jōkō (the Dinghai year), on the fifth day of the month of Dazou, while the old bhikṣu Junsoku of Izumi was reading and collating [this text] at the Chikuenken, he completed his marginal annotations and instructions, stating:

"Now, in the late summer of the ninth year of Kwanbun, I have again revised and polished this work to ensure its publication for the longevity of the world. Desiring to continue the lamp of the Dharma..."

May it forever illuminate the darkness of delusion and rescue all sentient beings, so that they may be distantly moistened by the wondrous Way. Having the misfortune of bathing in the ancestral grace, I reverently intend to offer my gratitude.
Thus says the Elder Beggar of Zhizhi Hall, the Venerable Nunetong.
